records.name: Ducts, lobules and the terminal duct lobular unit
records.tldr: Breast ducts connect to milk-producing acini, with supporting tissues around them. This anatomy helps interpret a sample but does not by itself establish cancer.
records.summary:
The breast contains an interconnected duct-lobular epithelial system within connective and fatty tissue. A terminal duct with its associated acini forms a terminal duct lobular unit. Tissue compartments and their proportions matter when interpreting imaging, microscopy or bulk molecular measurements. Histological diagnosis, grade, receptor status and disease extent require their own evidence.

NCI DCEG describes the TDLU as the origin of most breast cancer precursors and cancers. The names ductal and lobular are diagnostic morphology, not proof of an exact ancestral cell. Characteristic loss of E-cadherin in invasive lobular carcinoma reduces cell adhesion; diffuse growth in unconnected lines can make a lesion harder to feel or detect on imaging. The SEER description concerns this growth pattern rather than a universal test result for every lobular tumour.

Male breasts have ducts and may have lobules, but far fewer than female breasts; NCI describes lobular cancer as rare in men. Breast tissue and mammographic density change over life. Greater density is associated with higher breast-cancer risk and can obscure cancers on a mammogram; increasing age and childbearing are associated with lower density, alongside other influences. Mammographic density, TDLU involution and histological diagnosis are different observations.

notes: The terminal duct lobular unit contains a terminal duct and its associated acini. Acini make milk during lactation; ducts carry it towards the nipple. Lobules and larger lobes are different levels of organisation. Their size and abundance vary with physiology and life stage; an illustrative branch count is not a fixed anatomical count. A schematic grouping bracket is an annotation, not a tissue capsule or basement membrane. NCI DCEG describes TDLU involution with physiological ageing and completion of childbearing as reductions in acini per unit and total unit counts. This is an observational normal-tissue description, not a diagnostic rule for an individual.

From a typical normal acinus lumen outward, distinguish luminal epithelial cells, living myoepithelial cells, extracellular basement membrane and surrounding stroma. Stroma includes connective tissue, fat, vessels and immune cells. A basement membrane is neither a cell layer nor the plasma membrane around one cell.

An epithelial marker or abundant epithelial RNA can come from normal epithelium. A sample richer in glands and poorer in stroma can change a bulk measurement without a change within either cell type. Imaging, tissue morphology and protein staining observe different scales; a normal-breast atlas is a reference, not a stand-alone cancer diagnosis.

A quadrant or clock position locates a lesion. It does not identify its ancestral cell, receptor class or invasiveness. Likewise, ductal and lobular diagnostic names do not prove the precise ancestral location, and anatomical luminal position does not assign a molecular luminal subtype. A milk-flow diagram is not a cancer-progression sequence.

Ducts are epithelium-lined channels connected to milk-producing acini in lobules. The TDLU is a tissue unit, not one cell or a molecular subtype. Epithelial tissue can be normal, in situ or invasive: DCIS remains within the ductal boundary, whereas invasion enters surrounding tissue. In a fictional bulk assay, abundant epithelial RNA cannot establish invasion; that distinction needs tissue organisation, not simply epithelial abundance.

Milk ducts and lymphatic drainage are different networks. A quadrant or clock address supplies neither a drainage map nor lineage. Normal-anatomy drawings simplify scale, cell counts and branching; selected source text and captions support the arrangement illustrated, not a diagnosis or a universal number of cells.

In an invented normal-tissue cutaway, a larger duct connects to a terminal duct serving several hollow acini. The selected TDLU includes that terminal duct and its acini, excluding the larger duct. Each duct or acinus has its own epithelial boundary and basement membrane, with stroma around and between these structures. A bracket selects the group without adding a shared capsule. Magnifying one acinus shows a lumen, luminal epithelium, living nucleated myoepithelial cells, extracellular basement membrane and stroma rather than the whole lobule or breast. The branch count and magnification are chosen for the example.

records.tldr: Myoepithelial cells are living cells around normal breast ducts and acini; basement membrane is separate extracellular material outside them.
records.summary: These layers help organise normal breast structures and support pathological assessment of invasion. Their location, morphology, staining controls and diagnostic context matter more than a single positive or negative marker.

notes: Typical normal breast ducts and acini have luminal epithelial cells facing the lumen, an outer living myoepithelial layer, extracellular basement membrane and then stroma. Myoepithelial cells have contractile features that help move milk; they are not the chest muscle. Basement membrane contains matrix proteins such as laminins and type IV collagen, not living cells.

Basement membrane beneath an epithelial structure differs from plasma membrane around one cell. Cell polarity describes different inward and outward organisation. Gudjonsson and colleagues' human-cell culture experiments showed that normal myoepithelial cells or laminin-1 could restore luminal orientation in collagen gels; this is model evidence about organisation, not a demonstrated cancer treatment.

Myoepithelial immunohistochemistry is supporting evidence interpreted with morphology. p63 is nuclear; calponin and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain are cytoplasmic markers. Ask which cells stain, where they stain and whether technical controls work. A failed positive control undermines an apparently absent rim.

Werling and colleagues found gaps around some noninvasive structures, stromal staining with muscle-associated markers and p63 staining in some carcinoma cells. Gusterson and colleagues found basement-membrane proteins in some invasive carcinomas. Neither marker absence nor protein presence alone proves the tissue boundary. Basal-like RNA features also do not establish myoepithelial ancestry.

In Gusterson and colleagues' 1982 tissue study, laminin and type IV collagen were detected in normal breast, benign lesions and grade I invasive carcinomas but were absent from grade II and III infiltrating carcinomas in that study. That historical cohort does not make protein presence proof of an intact noninvasive boundary, or protein absence a universal grade rule.

Werling and colleagues examined 85 breast lesions. In that series, at least focal p63 staining in tumour cells occurred in 11% of cases, while stromal myofibroblasts stained with smooth muscle myosin heavy chain in 8% and calponin in 76%. Some noninvasive structures had gaps. These assay- and cohort-specific observations explain why localisation and controls matter; they are not universal diagnostic accuracy estimates.

CAP's morphology-based histological classification and supporting-marker assessment answer a tissue question. A schematic rim is neither an immunostain result nor a diagnosis; illustrated gaps or colours cannot establish invasion. Interpret the actual tissue architecture and appropriately controlled stains together.

records.name: Ki-67 index (proliferation by IHC)
records.tldr: The Ki-67 index is the percentage of evaluated tumour-cell nuclei that stain for a protein associated with the active cell cycle.
records.summary: Ki-67 immunohistochemistry reports the percentage of evaluated tumour-cell nuclei positive under the defined staining and scoring method. In gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours the WHO classification grades G1 (< 3 percent), G2 (3 to 20 percent) and G3 (> 20 percent). The FDA's March 3, 2023 breast-cancer expansion removed the Ki-67 testing requirement for the specified high-risk HR-positive, HER2-negative adjuvant abemaciclib indication. Trial cohort definitions are distinct from that regulatory testing rule. The International Ki67 in Breast Cancer Working Group limited its 2021 clinical-utility conclusion to selected anatomically favourable ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancers under standardised scoring, with prognosis assessment at 5 percent or less or 30 percent or more. These extremes are not universal thresholds for other cancers, methods or treatment decisions.

notes: Ki-67 is associated with active cell-cycle phases and is generally absent from resting G0 cells. Its immunohistochemical index is positive eligible tumour-cell nuclei divided by all eligible nuclei evaluated, expressed as a percentage. MIB-1 names an antibody. Staining intensity is not the denominator; 30 positive nuclei among 100 eligible nuclei gives 30% in that field.

Ki-67 is not a visible-mitosis count, a doubling time, a percentage growth per day, a recurrence probability or a complete Nottingham grade. A treatment-related decrease does not independently establish cell killing or patient benefit. RNA proliferation scores and protein immunostaining measure different features.

Sampling and aggregation change the estimate. With fictional fields containing 90 positive nuclei out of 900 and 50 out of 100, pooling gives 140/1000 = 14%; averaging the two field percentages gives 30%; selecting the second field gives 50%. These are different estimators. They do not reproduce the International Ki67 Working Group's calibrated, area-weighted global method.

Retain specimen, treatment time point, fixation, antibody/platform, counterstaining, controls, eligible nuclei and regional scoring rule. Poor visibility of negative nuclei can distort the denominator. The working group's weighted-global approach estimates areas with different staining levels and samples nuclei from those field types after calibration; it is not simply an unweighted hotspot average.

The 2021 working-group utility conclusion concerned anatomically favourable T1 to T2, N0 to N1, ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer under standardised methods, with limited prognosis use at the specified extremes. It did not establish a universal triple-negative treatment cutoff. CAP's September 2026 template treats breast Ki-67 testing as optional; do not transfer one assay's clinical rule to another cancer or setting.

The reviewed monarchE label defines cohort 1 by at least four positive axillary nodes, or one to three plus grade 3 or tumour size at least 50 mm. Cohort 1 was not defined by a mandatory Ki-67 threshold. Cohort 2 enrolled those not eligible for cohort 1 with one to three positive axillary nodes and centrally assessed Ki-67 at least 20% using MIB-1/Dako Omnis. The former regulatory testing requirement must not be mistaken for cohort 1 eligibility. This history is not a TNBC treatment rule.

An index is a snapshot of eligible nuclei in active cell-cycle phases. Net tumour growth also depends on cell loss and the duration of cell-cycle phases; the same index need not imply the same doubling time. Neither staining intensity nor percentage positive establishes a daily growth rate.

records.name: Lymph node status (node-positive / node-negative)
records.tldr: Lymph-node status classifies nodal involvement at a specified time and by a particular assessment. It does not measure every cancer cell throughout the body.
records.summary:
Clinical assessment before treatment and pathological assessment of removed nodes are different observations. Record the organ, method, timing, prefixes and modifiers rather than using positive or negative alone. A negative sampled-node result does not establish that every unsampled node is negative.

In the breast B-51 trial, clinical N1 described movable ipsilateral level I/II axillary involvement. Do not replace this clinical definition with a pathological one-to-three-node count. After neoadjuvant treatment, ypN0 is a pathological classification and can have modifiers. B-51 permitted ypN0i+ isolated tumour cells but did not collect their prevalence or specific outcomes.

The separate A011202 registry requires a nodal metastasis greater than 0.2 millimetres and treats deposits at or below 0.2 millimetres as N0i+. Those protocol rules do not make every use of positive or negative interchangeable. Nodal response alone is not a complete response in the breast or proof of whole-body clearance.

records.tldr: TNM describes primary tumour extent, regional nodes and distant metastasis under rules specific to the cancer and staging edition.
records.summary: Interpret TNM with the organ, system, edition, evidence and treatment moment attached. Clinical, surgery-first pathological and post-neoadjuvant categories describe different assessments. Anatomical groups and prognostic groups are distinct, and a stage does not independently predict an individual outcome or choose a treatment.

State system and disease-specific edition; AJCC breast remains eighth edition in the 2026 current-system table. In breast rules, T3 is larger than 5 cm, whereas T4 requires qualifying skin or chest-wall extension. Size alone cannot establish T4 or an overall stage group.

c denotes clinical assessment using examination, imaging and available biopsy evidence; p incorporates surgical pathological evidence. yc and yp identify clinical and pathological assessments after neoadjuvant treatment. Preserve the full treatment/specimen context: a later addendum on an old pretreatment biopsy still concerns that old sample.

Keep pretreatment and residual T/N records rather than splicing a pretreatment T to a post-treatment N. CAP applies the y prefix to a formal months-long preoperative endocrine course, but not a brief exposure of days or weeks. Negative breast and regional-node specimens cannot supply pM0; M0 is clinical and pM1 requires the applicable pathological evidence.

TNM categories do not alone specify a prognostic stage incorporating grade and receptors. Post-treatment extent and response are related but distinct. Regional nodal disease or extranodal extension does not by itself establish M1. In a fictional 6-cm pretreatment breast tumour without qualifying T4 features, cT3 can coexist with later ypT2 ypN1a without erasing the original extent.

In breast clinical classification, cN3b denotes combined ipsilateral internal mammary and axillary involvement, not a count of ten surgical nodes. With M0, anatomical IIIB comprises T4 with N0, N1 or N2; a T3 size alone does not make IIIB. These anatomical groups differ from grade/receptor-specific clinical prognostic groups.

Residual cancer burden combines breast-bed dimensions and cellularity with nodal count and metastasis diameter under its own protocol. It complements residual ypTNM rather than replacing it: a largest contiguous invasive focus for ypT is not interchangeable with a two-dimensional RCB bed.

records.name: Nottingham grade (breast cancer grade 1, 2 and 3)
records.tldr: Nottingham grade combines three microscopic feature scores into grade 1, 2 or 3. It describes invasive breast tissue and does not by itself establish disease extent.
records.summary: Nottingham histological grade combines tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic activity, each scored from 1 to 3. Totals 3 to 5 are grade 1, 6 to 7 grade 2 and 8 to 9 grade 3. CAP records component scores and the overall grade when grading is applicable; its template excludes microinvasion-only cases from grading. Mitotic assessment depends on a defined observation area and microscope calibration. In Elston and Ellis' 1991 Nottingham/Tenovus study, 1,831 of more than 2,200 patients with primary operable breast cancer were graded; grade 1 had better survival than grades 2 and 3 (P less than 0.0001). This observational prognostic evidence does not turn grade into stage or a treatment-benefit estimate.

notes: Grade is not the grade of a side effect. A treatment side effect is also given a grade, from 1 to 5, on a completely separate scale (see `toxicity-grade`). A grade 3 cancer and a grade 3 side effect have nothing to do with each other.

Nottingham grading of invasive breast carcinoma combines tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism and recognisable mitotic figures. Each receives 1 to 3 points: totals 3 to 5 give grade 1, 6 to 7 grade 2, and 8 to 9 grade 3. Thus assigned components 2, 3 and 3 sum to 8, grade 3; the sum is not a percentage.

Mitotic scoring uses ten consecutive high-power fields in the most mitotically active region, with field size calibrated for the microscope. Count recognisable division, excluding dark, fragmented or apoptotic nuclei. Equal raw counts over different observation areas need not receive the same score. Ki-67 staining does not replace the mitotic component.

Histological type describes morphology, grade scores microscopic features, and anatomical stage describes extent. Grade 3 does not mean stage III, low grade does not mean benign, and invasive Nottingham grading differs from DCIS nuclear grading. Grade can contribute to prognostic staging without becoming another measure of spread.

Retain the biopsy or resection, tissue region and treatment time point when comparing grades. Heterogeneity, limited tissue and treatment effects can restrict comparison. One section does not represent every tumour region, and grade alone supplies neither nodal/distant status nor a personal treatment-benefit estimate.

A nucleus contains a cell's genetic material. Nuclear pleomorphism means variation in nuclear size and appearance; a mitotic figure is a cell visibly dividing. These microscopic observations differ from Ki-67 protein staining, and a dark or dying nucleus should not simply be counted as division.

In CAP 4.11, tubule-formation scores 1, 2 and 3 correspond to greater than 75%, 10 to 75%, and less than 10% of tumour area forming glandular or tubular structures. Its nuclear descriptors compare with benign epithelial nuclei, alongside chromatin, nucleoli and variation in size and shape; a red-blood-cell diameter is not the comparator in that template. The reporting template marks microinvasion-only cases as not graded.

RCPath's November 2024 G148 dataset specifies the Nottingham method and recording its individual components for audit. It describes approximate grade 1:2:3 distributions of 2:3:5 in symptomatic and 3:5:2 in screen-detected cancers, as audit context rather than diagnostic quotas. It reports about 70% agreement between core-biopsy and corresponding surgical grades. Tubule assessment covers the tumour overall, while pleomorphism and mitoses use the worst area, often the periphery. If a higher-grade or morphologically different component in the resection was absent from the preoperative sample, the dataset recommends repeat receptor assays. These are source-specific reporting instructions, not an individual prognosis.

records.name: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) in breast cancer
records.tldr: Homologous recombination deficiency concerns impaired DNA repair. A genomic scar score, a BRCA finding and a functional assay provide different evidence; none alone guarantees benefit from a particular treatment.
records.summary: In the HRD scoring approach used in the studies below, three DNA-based measures of genomic instability (loss of heterozygosity, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale state transitions) are summed into an HRD score, with that study definition using a score of 42 or more or a BRCA1/2 mutation. This is not a universal cutoff for every HRD assay. In three neoadjuvant platinum trials in triple-negative disease, HR deficiency predicted residual cancer burden 0 or I and pathological complete response (odds ratios 4.96 and 6.52 in the platinum, gemcitabine and iniparib trial; 10.18 and 17.00 in two cisplatin trials), remained significant after adjustment for clinical variables, and identified responders among BRCA1/2 non-mutated tumours (Telli 2016). In GeparSixto, HRD was measured in 193 of 315 triple-negative participants: 136 (70.5 percent) were HR deficient, 82 of them (60.3 percent) with a high score but no tumour BRCA mutation; HR deficiency independently predicted pathological complete response (odds ratio 2.60), and adding carboplatin raised the rate from 33.9 to 63.5 percent in HR-deficient tumours but only from 20.0 to 29.6 percent in non-deficient tumours, with the interaction test not significant, so HRD predicted response but not carboplatin benefit; carboplatin improved disease-free survival in triple-negative disease overall (hazard ratio 0.56) (Loibl 2018). Beyond germline BRCA, olaparib produced confirmed responses in metastatic breast cancer with germline PALB2 mutations (objective response 82 percent, median progression-free survival 13.3 months) and somatic BRCA1/2 mutations (50 percent, 6.3 months) but none with ATM or CHEK2 mutations alone (TBCRC 048, Tung 2020). Regulatory use differs from ovarian cancer: NICE's adjuvant olaparib recommendation rests on a germline BRCA mutation (TA886), not an HRD score, and the platinum recommendation in NG101 1.8 applies to all triple-negative disease needing neoadjuvant chemotherapy, HRD-tested or not. The site's general HRD term and the hrd-positive readout carry the ovarian thresholds and assays.

notes: BRCAness is a research description of resemblance to BRCA-deficient cancers without a known BRCA mutation. Turner and colleagues' original concept was not one standard diagnostic assay. Similar repair marks can suggest a process worth investigating without identifying its cause, whether it is still present, or a future drug response. BRCA1/2 disruption and other mechanisms, including epigenetic changes in gene regulation, can affect repair; a BRCA-like pattern does not establish inheritance or make every repair-gene alteration equivalent.

Separate cause, history and function. Sequencing can identify a candidate disruption; genomic scars and classifiers describe patterns accumulated in DNA; a functional assay examines an activity under its measurement conditions. Watkins and colleagues' review warns that restoration of repair can make historical scars misleading about current function. That is a qualified interpretation of the biology, not a direct scar-persistence measurement in Cruz's patient series. An earlier high-scar sample and later RAD51 foci can therefore coexist without establishing that either measurement is wrong.

Waks and colleagues studied paired samples from eight selected patients with germline and/or somatic BRCA-altered metastatic breast cancer and acquired resistance to PARP inhibition or platinum. Four had definite or putative reversions and all four acquired RAD51 foci; six acquired foci overall, of whom three received another DNA-damaging therapy and all three were resistant. Those small, selected denominators support possible restoration mechanisms. They do not provide a population reversion frequency, a universal resistance test or a personal response probability.

Davies and colleagues' HRDetect classified BRCA-deficient genomic patterns, with 98.7% sensitivity in the study cohort of 560 breast cancers. Forty-seven additional tumours without known BRCA1/2 mutations had high model scores. That is a classifier result, not a measured probability of response or proof of the tumour's current repair function. Cruz and colleagues studied breast/ovarian tumour models and a small retrospective clinical set of ten tumours from eight patients. RAD51 foci were interpreted with cell-cycle and damage context; that work does not validate every RAD51 method or cutoff.

For an assay comparison, keep specimen and collection time, tumour content, named method/version, required DNA or tissue sections, and whether matched normal is needed. Sequencing-derived patterns, model scores and a percentage of assessable cells with RAD51 foci have different units. Poor genomic material, insufficient tumour, an old sample or too few cycling cells can make interpretation fail; in the Waks method, absent RAD51 with fewer than 3% geminin-positive cells was uninterpretable, not evidence of deficiency. Cutoffs do not transfer between methods.

As a fictional reading exercise, an earlier sample has a high genomic-scar result and a later sample has RAD51 foci under an assessable protocol. Record both dates, methods and denominators before asking which finding supports a cause, past history or present function. Neither result establishes constitutional origin, guarantees a response, proves that adding another drug helps, or settles trial entry. A drug-induced phenotype in a laboratory can motivate a hypothesis; clinical combination benefit requires evidence in the relevant treatment, population, comparator and endpoint.

records.name: Oligometastatic disease
records.tldr: Oligometastatic disease means a limited number of detected distant metastases under a stated definition. The count alone does not establish all disease is visible or that treating each site will produce a cure.
records.summary:
Oligometastatic disease describes limited detected distant spread, under a specified clinical or study definition. It is a hypothesis that some limited patterns may be amenable to treatment directed at all visible sites; a few visible lesions do not prove a distinct biology or the absence of microscopic disease. Regional lymph nodes alone are not distant metastases.

The ESTRO-ASTRO consensus describes one to five lesions, with every site safely treatable, while acknowledging that there is no universally established maximum. A consensus definition is not proof of added benefit. Treatment decisions require the cancer setting, prior burden and treatment, comparator, endpoint, safety and the person's goals.

notes: A few lit windows show what is detectable, not a census of every room. This analogy does not mean that every limited pattern conceals widespread disease. Synchronous metastases are detected near the initial diagnosis; metachronous metastases are detected later, with the interval defined by the author or protocol. Induced limited disease follows previously widespread disease and systemic treatment. Oligoprogression means a growing subset while other disease remains controlled during treatment. Limited residual or persistent disease means limited visible disease remains after treatment; specify whether it is stable or progressing. These labels are not universal synonyms.

The SABR-COMET randomised phase 2 study enrolled 99 selected patients with different primary cancers, including 18 with breast cancer, a controlled primary and one to five treatable metastases. Its extended follow-up found eight-year overall survival of 27.2% with SABR plus standard care versus 13.6% with standard care alone, with grade 2 or higher acute or late toxicity of 30.3% versus 9.1%. This mixed-cancer result is not a definitive TNBC treatment effect. Control of an irradiated site, delay in progression, survival and symptom relief are different outcomes.

NRG-BR002 tested adding ablation to first-line systemic therapy in breast cancer with at most four metastases, controlled primary disease, at most 12 months of first-line therapy without progression, and all visible sites amenable to SBRT or resection. Of 129 enrolled patients, 125 were eligible for analysis and 79% had HR-positive/HER2-negative disease. In the protocol-specified phase 2 go/no-go analysis with a December 20, 2021 data cutoff, median progression-free survival was 23.0 months without ablation and 19.5 months with it; the hazard ratio was 0.92, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.57 to 1.47 and stratified P = .42. Overall survival did not differ significantly and the study did not proceed to phase 3. This does not supply a definitive effect for every subtype or erase a separate symptom-relief goal.

Classification uses the imaging and its coverage and sensitivity, lesion and organ counts, locations, sizes, dates, previous burden, systemic treatment and response or progression history. A biopsy may be needed to confirm a finding, but classification is not inherently a tumour-consuming molecular assay. Benign mimics, undetected lesions and missing earlier records can mislead. Keep a protocol's count, timing, primary-control and treatability requirements; five lesions is not a cure cutoff and a molecular result does not universally establish this state.

Three fictional histories can each contain two lesions now: two newly detected metastases with no earlier distant disease, two residual lesions after treatment of many, or two growing sites amid many stable sites during therapy. The numeral counts a different subset in each history. Keep the earlier burden and dates rather than merging these groups. A response-selected group and a progression-selected group answer different questions; curative intent is a documented goal whose success needs long-term outcome measurement, not an inference from the current count.

NRG-BR002's accessible NIH author manuscript distinguishes its protocol-specified phase 2 analysis from non-protocol-specified extended follow-up with a September 4, 2025 cutoff. The latter reported median progression-free survival of 23.0 months without ablation versus 29.5 with it, hazard ratio 0.93, 95% confidence interval 0.60 to 1.44, and overall-survival hazard ratio 0.94, interval 0.56 to 1.60. These are separate analyses, not interchangeable updates to one median. The indexed abstract reports overall-survival hazard ratio 1.07 and stratified P = .52. Fifty-six of sixty assigned to ablation received SBRT, about 93%; this was not BOOSTER's probe-based comparison. Table 1 has ten triple-negative participants among 125, 8%, and 99 with hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative cancer. The report does not precisely establish every subtype's effect, and confidence intervals crossing one do not prove zero effect. The authors' recommendation against routine use outside trials retains a separate palliation exception.

records.name: Brain metastases (secondary brain tumours)
records.tldr: Brain metastases are cancers that have spread to the brain from elsewhere, most often from the lung, breast or skin. Focused radiation aimed at each spot (radiosurgery) has largely replaced radiation to the whole brain, and for some cancers modern targeted drugs and immunotherapy reach the brain well enough to shrink the deposits on their own.
records.summary:
Brain metastases seed the grey-white junction and watershed zones through the arterial circulation; they are recognised on contrast MRI and, with a known primary, rarely need biopsy. Prognosis depends on the primary, its molecular subtype, performance status, extracranial disease and number of lesions (graded prognostic assessment). Dexamethasone relieves oedema. Management has moved in twenty years from whole-brain radiotherapy for nearly everyone to a choice among surgery, stereotactic radiosurgery, systemic therapy with brain penetration and, for some, no brain-directed treatment at all.

Surgery is used for a large or symptomatic single lesion or when tissue is needed (Patchell, 1990), followed by radiosurgery to the cavity rather than whole-brain radiotherapy (N107C, 2017). For a limited number of metastases, Alliance N0574 (JAMA 2016) showed that adding whole-brain radiotherapy to radiosurgery worsened cognition at three months in 91.7 percent of patients against 63.5 percent with radiosurgery alone, without lengthening survival, and radiosurgery alone is now standard for up to four lesions and increasingly for more. When whole-brain radiotherapy is still used, NRG CC001 (JCO 2020) showed hippocampal avoidance with memantine preserves cognition. QUARTZ (Lancet 2016) found no meaningful gain in quality-adjusted survival from whole-brain radiotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer patients unsuited to surgery or radiosurgery, so best supportive care alone is legitimate in poor-prognosis patients.

Systemic therapy now controls brain disease in several subtypes: osimertinib in EGFR-mutant and lorlatinib in ALK-positive lung cancer (CROWN), tucatinib with trastuzumab and capecitabine (HER2CLIMB) and trastuzumab deruxtecan (DESTINY-Breast12) in HER2-positive breast cancer, nivolumab plus ipilimumab in melanoma (CheckMate 204) and dabrafenib plus trametinib in BRAF-mutant melanoma (COMBI-MB), so asymptomatic small metastases in these groups are often treated with drugs first and radiosurgery held in reserve. Trials have historically excluded patients with brain metastases; their inclusion, the management of leptomeningeal disease, radionecrosis after radiosurgery, and drugs designed to cross the blood-brain barrier are the open fronts.

notes: A breast-cancer deposit in the brain remains metastatic breast cancer, not a new primary brain cancer. Parenchymal metastases involve brain tissue; leptomeningeal spread involves the thin tissue layers covering the brain and spinal cord. A study of CNS events may include both. Spread and successful growth require several biological steps. In Lockman's two mouse breast-cancer models, blood-tumour barrier permeability and drug uptake varied between and within metastases. This does not establish that every human brain deposit excludes every drug or that all drugs penetrate equally.

The denominator and starting clock change a brain-risk estimate. Lin and colleagues identified 116 patients treated for metastatic TNBC at one centre in 2000 to 2006: 14% had CNS involvement at metastatic diagnosis and 46% were diagnosed with it before death. Their CNS definition included parenchymal and leptomeningeal disease, and ascertainment was mostly symptom-led. Dawood and colleagues instead studied 2,448 stage I to III TNBC patients diagnosed in 1990 to 2010: the cumulative incidence of brain metastasis as first recurrence was 3.7% at two years and 5.4% at five years from diagnosis, treating death or another first recurrence as competing events. These are different selected populations and endpoints, not interchangeable early-disease and metastatic risks.

Martin and colleagues' population-based study concerned invasive breast cancer diagnosed in 2010 to 2013 and brain metastases recorded at initial diagnosis, including subtype analyses. It was not a lifetime event study. To interpret any such estimate, retain imaging and clinical-record definitions, diagnosis and event dates, follow-up time, deaths, losses and any context-specific biopsy confirmation. Distinguish a diagnosis-time proportion, events per patient-time and cumulative incidence during a stated period. Referral patterns, missed asymptomatic disease, subtype definitions and incomplete follow-up can change what is observed. Historical cohorts cannot calibrate a modern individual forecast or establish a universal subtype ranking or screening interval.

Death can prevent a later brain event and is therefore a competing event, not ordinary loss to follow-up. Likewise, first brain recurrence differs from any brain involvement after other recurrence. A reported share of recurrences with brain involvement needs the original patient denominator before it can describe patient risk. A cohort association does not itself validate a personal calculator or show that scheduled earlier detection improves survival.

In a fictional cohort of 100 people with complete follow-up for two years from enrolment, 20 recur and five of those 20 have a brain event. The same five are 25% of those who recur and 5% of all enrolled people. Each person is counted once, with the five nested within the 20, not added as five more. These raw fractions assume complete observation; they are not competing-risk estimates. Restarting the clock at recurrence would ask a different question. Before applying a percentage, name the population, event, starting point, time window and follow-up method.

records.name: HER2-positive (IHC 3+ or ISH-amplified)
records.tldr: HER2-positive breast cancer has an integrated result showing HER2 protein overexpression or gene amplification under the applicable testing rules. The result is separate from eligibility for a specific medicine.
records.summary:
Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) is a cell-surface receptor protein encoded by ERBB2. Gene amplification, protein abundance measured by immunohistochemistry and RNA expression are different observations. In invasive breast cancer, HER2 status integrates the IHC pattern and indicated in-situ hybridisation workup under the applicable guideline. IHC 2+ is equivocal, not half-positive or a completed negative result.

A HER2-positive result and a HER2-enriched RNA subtype are not interchangeable. HER2-low or ultralow staining remains negative for overexpression/amplification in the relevant breast context, while some specified treatment settings use low expression to select an antibody-drug conjugate. A signalling receptor can also serve as a delivery address; neither the label nor one staining category proves pathway dependence, eligibility or individual drug benefit.

notes: The September 2026 CAP template distinguishes negative IHC 0 with no detected membrane staining from negative 0+ with faint, incomplete staining in at most 10% of tumour cells. IHC 1+ has faint incomplete staining in more than 10%. A common 2+ pattern is weak to moderate complete staining in more than 10%, but intense complete staining in at most 10% and some incomplete patterns also need workup. IHC 3+ requires intense complete membrane staining in more than 10% of a homogeneous contiguous invasive tumour-cell population. This abbreviated map does not replace the full rules for unusual patterns, artefacts and heterogeneity.

Tissue IHC and ISH use sections from an identified specimen/block. IHC reports a membrane pattern category; ISH uses nucleic-acid probes in tissue to assess gene copies. A dual-probe ISH report retains counted cells, mean HER2 signals per cell, mean CEP17 signals per cell and the HER2/CEP17 ratio. In the Abbott PathVysion assay, CEP17 probes an alpha-satellite sequence in chromosome 17's centromeric region. The ratio is dimensionless and differs from the mean HER2 count; neither alone substitutes for the integrated algorithm, concurrent IHC and indicated recounting. Keep preservation, controls and distinct tumour populations visible in the interpretation.

A drawing of a few cells can illustrate complete versus incomplete membrane staining and intensity, but it is not a counted field or a scoring standard. In a fictional comparison, the same faint incomplete pattern in at most 10% versus more than 10% changes 0+ to 1+ under the specified template; it does not establish drug eligibility. For another fictional completed report, IHC 2+, ratio 1.8, mean HER2 3.5 signals per cell and an integrated ISH-negative finding fit the HER2-negative, low-expression range. The ratio is not 1.8 copies and the example is not a complete algorithm or a medicine decision.

Read the measurement sequence as IHC pattern, ISH when indicated, integrated status, then a separate evidence and eligibility question. IHC 0 does not mean literally zero protein molecules. An ERBB2 mutation, amplification, RNA abundance, a HER2-enriched expression label and surface protein staining cannot stand in for one another. HER2-low staining can occur within receptor-defined TNBC. Method, setting and treatment-specific evidence remain necessary.

The RCPath UK breast dataset retains a different classification from ASCO/CAP for some dual-probe ISH group 2 cases: HER2/CEP17 ratio at least 2.0 with mean HER2 below 4 signals per cell. The UK dataset classifies these as positive. Under ASCO/CAP, concurrent IHC matters: IHC 3+ is positive, while IHC 2+ requires the specified recount and is negative if the same group persists; IHC 0 or 1+ is negative. Thus the US result is not uniformly negative from the ratio and copy number alone. The UK dataset asks for ratio and mean HER2 and CEP17 signals, with the guideline and specimen context retained.

records.name: Basal-like breast cancer
records.tldr: Basal-like describes a breast-cancer gene-expression pattern. It overlaps with receptor-defined triple-negative disease, but the labels use different measurements and are not interchangeable.
records.summary: Perou and colleagues profiled 65 surgical specimens from 42 patients on cDNA microarrays of 8,102 genes and found the tumours could be classified into subtypes distinguished by pervasive differences in gene expression, the origin of the intrinsic subtypes luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like and normal-like (Perou 2000). The Cancer Genome Atlas integrated copy number, methylation, exome, mRNA, microRNA and protein data across primary breast cancers, confirmed four main classes, found TP53, PIK3CA and GATA3 the only genes mutated in more than 10 percent overall, and showed basal-like tumours share many molecular features with high-grade serous ovarian cancer, implying a related aetiology and similar therapeutic opportunities (TCGA 2012). Triple-negative and basal-like overlap but are not identical: of 412 triple-negative tumours 21.4 percent were non-basal-like, and of 473 basal-like tumours 31.5 percent were not triple-negative; triple-negative tumours classified as luminal or HER2-enriched had expression profiles indistinguishable from their non-triple-negative counterparts, most HER2-enriched triple-negative tumours lacked HER2 amplification, and the authors suggest triple-negative trials stratify by basal-like versus non-basal-like expression (Prat 2013). In the population-based Carolina Breast Cancer Study, using immunohistochemical surrogates (ER, PR and HER2 negative with cytokeratin 5/6 or HER1 positive), basal-like tumours were found in 39 percent of premenopausal African American women against 14 percent of postmenopausal African American and 16 percent of non-African American women; they had more TP53 mutations (44 against 15 percent), higher mitotic index and grade, and among the shortest breast cancer-specific survival (Carey 2006). Basal-like cancers are the typical cancer of BRCA1 carriers, and adenoid cystic carcinoma is a special type of basal-like tumour with an excellent outlook (Ghabach 2010), a reminder that an expression label does not establish a uniform behaviour or exact cell ancestry. PAM50 basal-like and Lehmann BL1/BL2 belong to different classifiers; a PAM50 basal-like call does not by itself assign either Lehmann profile.

A label or pathway-enrichment pattern alone does not establish functional dependence or benefit from a particular treatment.

A normal-like or basal-like classifier output is not a diagnosis of benign tissue or proof of origin in a mature basal cell. The research classifier, receptor tests and histology remain separately interpretable.

Basal-marker immunohistochemistry provides contextual protein evidence, not a stand-alone subtype from ribonucleic acid (RNA) or an exact lineage trace. SOX10 is the gene symbol for SRY-box transcription factor 10; the encoded protein is a transcription factor whose tissue assay commonly assesses nuclear signal. CK5/6 denotes cytokeratins 5 and 6, epithelial structural proteins, while EGFR means epidermal growth factor receptor and is also called HER1. Nielsen and colleagues evaluated an ER, HER2, CK5/6 and EGFR protein surrogate against expression-defined basal-like cancers and in a historical tissue series. A specified research panel is not equivalent to one marker reproducing a full RNA classifier.

Cimino-Mathews and colleagues found SOX10 nuclear staining in normal myoepithelial cells and in a subset of selected triple-negative and metaplastic breast carcinomas. Their series had 100 invasive cancers, with 38 of 58 basal-like, unclassified TNBC or metaplastic cases staining, compared with two of 42 luminal/HER2 cases. These selected-series frequencies are not universal prevalence or diagnostic sensitivity. SOX10 also occurs in other tumours, including melanoma and peripheral nerve-sheath tumours. Positive staining alone does not prove breast origin, and a negative result does not exclude breast carcinoma.

Ask which cells carry the signal before interpreting a stain. Two fictional sketches can show SOX10-positive nuclei in benign myoepithelial cells around a duct and in a separate malignant-cell region. They are illustrations, not micrographs, positivity cutoffs or proof from anatomy alone. In a fictional axillary SOX10-positive mass, identify the intended cells and localisation, morphology, other markers and clinical context before assigning an origin. SOX10 does not by itself establish breast origin, basal-like RNA, Lehmann BL1, ancestry, treatment dependence or vaccine benefit.

A stain report needs the tissue/lesion and selected cells, fixation, antibody and protocol, nuclear or other expected localisation, scoring rule, presence, intensity and percentage among the intended cells. Appropriate positive and negative controls, including interpretable internal tissue controls, are needed. Preservation, scant tumour, background and staining of neighbouring benign cells can limit interpretation. Protein presence is not direct transcription-factor activity, an RNA classifier, lineage tracing or a drug-response assay. The percentage of stained tumour cells is not the probability that a treatment will work. Associations with outcome in a tissue cohort do not establish added benefit from a treatment.

records.name: TNBC molecular subtyping
records.tldr: TNBC RNA subtyping compares gene-expression patterns under a named research classifier. Tissue mixture, method and version matter, and the result is separate from receptor tests or a treatment choice.
records.summary:
Lehmann's original TNBCtype system described six expression groups: BL1, BL2, IM, M, MSL and LAR. The 2016 TNBCtype-4 refinement retained BL1, BL2, M and LAR as tumour-focused profiles after evaluating immune and stromal contributions to the IM and MSL signals. Removed-profile samples were reassigned to their second-highest correlated tumour-profile centroid, not automatically to M.

BL1 is associated with cell-cycle/DNA-damage-response programmes; BL2 with growth-factor and myoepithelial-associated expression; M with motility and differentiation; and LAR with luminal and androgen-related transcription. These are classifier associations, not proof of one cause, functional repair deficiency or dependence on an inhibitor.

A mixed-tissue IM signal and a BL1 call from an enriched preparation can coexist without proving tumour evolution. Compare preparation, method and scores. Tumour-focused labels do not make every bulk input free of immune or stromal RNA.
PAM50 basal-like, AR protein positivity, an RNA LAR label, histology and receptor-defined TNBC are separate measurements. A lineage-associated programme does not establish an exact cell of origin.

The defining cell-model and retrospective chemotherapy studies generated treatment hypotheses. Prospective strategy research also exists: FUTURE-SUPER used a distinct Fudan classifier plus genomic biomarkers and compared matched regimens with nab-paclitaxel alone. Its pooled phase 2 result does not validate every same-named profile or isolate the value of a classifier from its treatment bundle.

records.name: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)
aka: ER negative PR negative HER2 negative
records.tldr: A breast cancer classified as oestrogen receptor-negative, progesterone receptor-negative and HER2-negative by the relevant tests. Negative test categories do not mean that every receptor molecule is absent.
records.summary:
TNBC is defined by negative ER, PR and HER2 test classifications: ER and PR nuclear staining below 1 percent, and HER2-negative results under the applicable IHC/ISH algorithm. These classifications do not establish the complete absence of receptor molecules. It is biologically heterogeneous (including distinct RNA expression profiles and histologies), often TP53-mutant, frequently HRD-positive (11 to 17% germline BRCA1/2 by cohort), and can express TROP2. Expression and cellular composition vary between tumours and need the sampled tissue and assay context. Relapses cluster in the first three years and favour visceral and brain metastases.

The standard of care changed three times in six years. KEYNOTE-522 (2020-21) made pembrolizumab plus carboplatin-containing chemotherapy before surgery, continued after, the standard for stage II-III disease, with a 4.9-point overall survival gain at five years (86.6% against 81.7%). OlympiA (2021) added adjuvant olaparib for germline BRCA carriers with residual disease. In metastatic disease, pembrolizumab-chemotherapy (CPS ≥10) was joined by the TROP2 ADCs: sacituzumab govitecan (ASCENT, reported in 2021; first-line ASCENT-03/04 2026) and datopotamab deruxtecan (TROPION-Breast02, first-line PD-1-ineligible, 2026, with an overall survival benefit), while trastuzumab deruxtecan has a specified advanced-breast HER2-low use after prior chemotherapy. The separate HR-positive ultralow use after endocrine therapy does not extend to TNBC. The EGFR×HER3 bispecific ADC iza-bren posted the first positive phase 3 for a bispecific ADC in pretreated TNBC in February 2026.

What remains unsolved: residual disease after KEYNOTE-522 (RCB II-III) still carries a high relapse risk (before immunotherapy, ten-year relapse-free survival was 55% for RCB-II and 23% for RCB-III, Symmans 2017); ADC sequencing (TOP1-payload cross-resistance) is unstudied; PD-L1-negative early disease has immunotherapy proven only in KEYNOTE-522's unselected population; brain metastases; and response and resistance within mesenchymal or claudin-low patterns need setting-specific evidence. Research directions include ADC + IO first line, de-escalation guided by TILs and pCR, ctDNA-guided escalation, TROP2 PET selection, next-generation ADCs with non-TOP1 or dual payloads, and personalised vaccines in the adjuvant setting.

Research expression subtyping, receptor tests, histology and inherited-risk results describe different axes. The 2016 TNBCtype-4 refinement retained BL1, BL2, M and LAR after investigating immune and stromal contributions to the older IM/MSL signals. A research label alone does not establish treatment sensitivity. Prospective strategies using other classifiers retain their own assay, matching rules, population and regimens.

How common it is, world and United States. No registry publishes a world count of triple-negative disease; the share has to be applied to breast cancer as a whole. The IARC breast fact sheet, served today with the GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates, gives 2,434,087 new breast cancers a year (the second commonest cancer, age-standardised rate 47.8 per 100,000) and 693,660 deaths (fourth, 12.9 per 100,000), with 45.1 percent of cases in Asia, 22.3 percent in Europe, 13.2 percent in Northern America, 9.3 percent in Africa and 9.0 percent in Latin America and the Caribbean. The triple-negative share in registries with receptor data runs from 8.4 percent of 1,151,724 US cases in 2010 to 2014 (Scott 2019) through 10.8 percent of all US cases, including those of unknown subtype, in SEER 21, 2019 to 2023 (the SEER subtype fact sheet), 12.2 percent of cases with known status in 2010 (Howlader 2014) and 12 percent in 2012 to 2016 (Howard and Olopade 2021), to around 15 percent on the Cancer Research UK patient page and 17 percent of 15,204 women treated at NCCN centres in 2000 to 2006 (Lin 2012). Applied to 2.4 million, a share of 10 to 15 percent would be about 240,000 to 370,000 people a year; that is arithmetic on the figures above, not a published count. In the United States the age-adjusted rate of hormone receptor-negative, HER2-negative breast cancer is 14.3 per 100,000 women a year against 132.5 for all breast cancer (SEER 21, 2019 to 2023), and 321,910 new female breast cancers of all subtypes are projected for 2026.

Who gets it. Age: triple-negative tumours are diagnosed younger than hormone receptor-positive tumours. Women under 40 had 1.53 times the odds of the triple-negative phenotype in the California registry (Bauer 2007) and 1.95 times the odds relative to women aged 50 to 64 in US Cancer Statistics (Scott 2019); Howlader found triple-negative patients 10 to 30 percent less likely to be diagnosed at older ages and 6.4 to 20 times more likely to present with high-grade disease; Cancer Research UK says the type develops more often in women under 40. Ethnicity: in SEER 21 (2019 to 2023) the rate of hormone receptor-negative, HER2-negative disease is 25.7 per 100,000 in non-Hispanic Black women against 13.0 in non-Hispanic White, 12.5 in Hispanic, 11.4 in American Indian and Alaska Native and 10.5 in Asian and Pacific Islander women, roughly a two-fold difference; non-Hispanic Black women had 2.27 times the odds of a triple-negative diagnosis in 2010 to 2014 (Scott 2019); the basal-like subtype was found in 39 percent of premenopausal African American women against 16 percent of non-African American women in the Carolina Breast Cancer Study (Carey 2006); and in 507 women in Nigeria and Senegal, triple-negative disease (basal-like 27 percent plus unclassified 28 percent) predominated, with a mean age of 44.8 (Huo 2009). In the UK, the POSH cohort of women diagnosed at 40 or under found triple-negative tumours in 26.1 percent of Black against 18.6 percent of White patients (Copson 2014), and an analysis of 116,500 women in England (2013 to 2018) found greater adjusted odds of ER-negative, high-grade and high-stage tumours in ethnic minority women, most marked in Black African and Black Caribbean women (Gathani 2021). Even after adjustment for stage, treatment delay and socioeconomic factors, African American women with triple-negative disease remain nearly twice as likely to die of it (Howard and Olopade 2021). Inherited risk: 57.1 percent of breast cancers in BRCA1 carriers were triple-negative against 23.3 percent in BRCA2 carriers and 13.8 percent in non-carriers (Atchley 2008); in 6,893 carriers the triple-negative share fell with age at diagnosis in BRCA1 and rose in BRCA2 carriers, and medullary tumours were BRCA1-related (Mavaddat 2012). Looked at from the other side, 14.6 percent of 1,824 triple-negative patients unselected for family history carried a deleterious mutation in one of 17 genes, 8.5 percent BRCA1, 2.7 percent BRCA2 and 1.2 percent PALB2 (Couch 2015); a prospective US registry found 15.4 percent with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, 27.6 percent among those diagnosed at 50 or under, 11.4 percent at 51 to 60 and 4.9 percent at 61 or over (Sharma 2014); and 12 percent of 2,733 UK women with breast cancer at 40 or under carried a BRCA mutation (Copson 2018). Cancer Research UK puts the lifetime breast cancer risk of a BRCA1 or BRCA2 carrier at 45 to 65 percent by age 70, with about 1 in 450 women carrying a mutation; PALB2 carries a relative risk of 7.18 and a 53 percent risk to age 80 (Yang 2020).

United Kingdom (Cancer Research UK, drawing on the four national registries). Breast cancer is the commonest cancer, with 59,413 new cases a year (2019 and 2021 to 2022), about 59,000 in females and 420 in males, 15 percent of all cancers; a quarter are diagnosed at 75 or over; incidence rates have risen 20 percent since the early 1990s and are projected to fall 1 percent by 2038 to 2040 while the count rises to about 70,300 a year; incidence rates are lower in the Asian and Black ethnic groups than the White group in England (2013 to 2017), which sits beside the higher triple-negative share in Black women noted above. There are about 11,200 deaths a year (2022 to 2024), the fourth commonest cause of cancer death and the second in women; mortality rates have fallen 46 percent since the early 1970s. In England in 2022, 85 percent of cases with a known stage were stage I or II; in 2019, 53 percent were diagnosed through an urgent suspected cancer referral, 32 percent through screening and 4 percent after an emergency presentation. About 23 percent of UK breast cancers are judged preventable, 8 percent attributed to alcohol and 1 percent to ionising radiation. Cancer Research UK does not publish a separate UK incidence count for triple-negative disease; the around 15 percent share on its patient page, and the 20 percent share in the young-onset POSH cohort (558 of 2,733), are the UK figures found for this record.

Risk factors that separate triple-negative from other breast cancers. Reproduction runs the other way from hormone receptor-positive disease: in 23,353 cases and 71,072 controls pooled across 31 studies, parous women had a lower risk of every luminal and HER2-enriched-like subtype but a higher risk of triple-negative disease immediately after a birth (odds ratio 3.12 for multiparous women right after their last birth), attenuating over decades (Jung 2022); in African American women parity raised triple-negative risk (odds ratio 1.37) while breastfeeding lowered ER-negative risk (0.81), and ER-negative risk rose with each birth in women who had not breastfed (1.68 for four or more births) (Palmer 2014). Cancer Research UK's summary that triple-negative disease is not associated with parity, from an older meta-analysis, is recorded beside these newer pooled analyses. Obesity: triple-negative cases were more often obese than hormone receptor-positive cases (odds ratio 1.20 case-case, 1.24 case-control), a signal confined to premenopausal women (1.43) in an 11-study meta-analysis (Pierobon 2013), and 1.89 in an Atlanta case series (Trivers 2009); Cancer Research UK notes the postmenopausal body-mass effect is largely limited to ER- and PR-positive tumours (adult weight gain raised ER- and PR-negative risk by 34 percent against 133 percent for positive tumours). Age at first birth and at menarche, and oral contraceptive or HRT use, are associated mainly with hormone receptor-positive tumours (CRUK risk page). A first-degree relative with breast cancer doubles breast cancer risk of any type, and the germline factors above (BRCA1 above all, then PALB2 and BRCA2) are the strongest known triple-negative risk factors. What is shared with all breast cancer: alcohol (8 percent of UK cases), ionising radiation (1 percent) and breast density (3 to 5 times the risk in the most dense breasts).

How it presents. Symptoms are those of any breast cancer: a lump or thickening in the breast or armpit, a change in size, shape or feel, skin puckering, dimpling, a rash or redness, fluid from the nipple, or a nipple that turns in (Cancer Research UK triple-negative and symptoms pages). What differs is the route and the tempo. Triple-negative tumours are less often found by a screening mammogram (29 percent against 48 percent of hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative tumours in NCCN centres) and present with a higher tumour category but are less likely to involve the lymph nodes (Lin 2012); they are over-represented among interval cancers, which appear between screens and carry worse prognostic features than screen-detected cancers (Houssami 2017); and they are more often high grade (Howlader 2014). Relapse is early: in 1,601 Toronto patients the triple-negative group had 2.6 times the hazard of distant recurrence and 3.2 times the hazard of death within five years but not afterwards, with the risk of distant recurrence peaking at about three years and falling rapidly (Dent 2007); recurrence and death rates were higher only in the first three years in the MD Anderson neoadjuvant series, which also found more visceral and fewer bone relapses (Liedtke 2008); and in 116 patients with metastatic disease treated in 2000 to 2006, 46 percent developed brain metastases before death and median survival from the metastatic diagnosis was 13.3 months (Lin 2008), a figure that the later trials in the treatment rows have moved. NICE NG12 (1.4) asks GPs to refer on the suspected cancer pathway anyone aged 30 or over with an unexplained breast lump, anyone 50 or over with discharge, retraction or other change in one nipple, and to consider it for skin changes or an unexplained axillary lump at 30 or over.

How it is diagnosed. In the UK the GP refers to a one-stop breast clinic for triple assessment: examination, mammogram, ultrasound and a needle core (or vacuum-assisted) biopsy, with axillary ultrasound and needle biopsy of any abnormal node (Cancer Research UK tests page). NICE NG101 (1.3.1 to 1.3.4) requires ER, PR and HER2 status to be assessed simultaneously on every invasive breast cancer at the initial histopathological diagnosis, by standardised, quality-assured immunohistochemistry reported quantitatively, and recorded at the preoperative and postoperative multidisciplinary meetings. Triple-negative is then a laboratory definition: ER negative when fewer than 1 percent of tumour nuclei stain, PR likewise, with 1 to 10 percent reported as a new ER Low Positive category on which endocrine benefit is uncertain (ASCO/CAP 2020, Allison); HER2 negative when immunohistochemistry is 0 or 1+, or 2+ with no amplification on in situ hybridisation (ASCO/CAP 2018, Wolff). The 2023 ASCO-CAP update kept those categories but added a reporting comment because the difference between HER2 0 and 1+ now decides eligibility for trastuzumab deruxtecan (Wolff 2023). NG101 defines triple-negative simply as ER, PR and HER2 each scored negative under local multidisciplinary team rules. ER-low positive disease can share features with ER-negative disease, but remains ER-positive and may benefit from endocrine treatment; selected cohort comparisons do not establish identical behaviour for every tumour: ER 1 to 10 percent tumours matched ER-negative tumours for germline BRCA prevalence, response and survival in a US registry (Yoder 2022) and in an Italian series (Dieci 2021), and Sweden treats ER 1 to 9 percent HER2-negative tumours as triple-negative, with 9.9 percent of 5,655 such cancers in 2008 to 2020 falling in that band (Acs 2024). Breast MRI is not routine before surgery but is offered when the extent of disease is unclear, when breast density defeats mammography, or to size an invasive lobular cancer (NG101 1.2). Staging tests beyond the breast and axilla, where the stage or symptoms warrant, are CT, bone scan, liver ultrasound or PET-CT, and blood tests including CA 15-3 which cannot diagnose or direct treatment on its own (Cancer Research UK tests page). NG101 (1.3.6) adds one test that applies to this subtype alone: offer germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing to women under 50 with triple-negative breast cancer, including those with no family history.

What the pathologist sees. Most triple-negative cancers are invasive carcinomas of no special type (the term the 2019 WHO classification, 5th edition, uses for what was called ductal carcinoma) of grade 3, with a high proliferation index: the Swedish cohort's median Ki-67 was 63 percent in ER-zero and 60 percent in ER-low tumours, and 80.8 percent of ER-zero tumours were grade III (Acs 2024). By gene expression, 78.6 percent of triple-negative tumours are basal-like and 21.4 percent belong to other intrinsic subtypes, while 31.5 percent of basal-like tumours are not triple-negative (Prat 2013); basal-like tumours share many molecular features with high-grade serous ovarian cancer, and TP53 is the mutation that recurs across them (TCGA 2012). Within the triple-negative group, Lehmann's 2011 analysis of 587 cases found six expression subtypes (basal-like 1 and 2, immunomodulatory, mesenchymal, mesenchymal stem-like and luminal androgen receptor), refined in 2016 to four tumour-intrinsic subtypes once the immunomodulatory and stem-like signals were traced to infiltrating lymphocytes and stroma; Burstein's four (luminal androgen receptor, mesenchymal, basal-like immunosuppressed and basal-like immune-activated) overlap them. Each has a page linked from this record. The WHO classification also names special histological types that are usually triple-negative: metaplastic carcinoma (70.3 percent triple-negative in 2,451 US cases, Ong 2018), carcinoma with medullary pattern (no longer a separate type in the 5th edition, Thomas 2023; Cserni 2020), adenoid cystic carcinoma (95 percent localised at diagnosis, 15-year relative survival 91.4 percent, Ghabach 2010), apocrine carcinoma (ER and PR negative, androgen receptor positive, Vranic 2013) and secretory carcinoma (ETV6-NTRK3 fusion in 92 percent, Tognon 2002). Rare subtypes together are 5 to 10 percent of triple-negative cancers (Thomas 2023), and the European Working Group for Breast Screening Pathology concludes that patients with the indolent pure forms (classical adenoid cystic, low-grade adenosquamous, fibromatosis-like metaplastic, secretory, acinic cell, tall cell with reversed polarity) are unlikely to benefit from chemotherapy (Cserni 2021). Stromal tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes are scored on the biopsy, and PD-L1 combined positive score is tested when metastatic treatment is planned (the glossary terms carry the thresholds).

How it is staged. The TNM 8th edition (2017) is the usual system in the UK, and Cancer Research UK sets it out in plain words. T1 is 2 cm or less (T1mi 0.1 cm or less, T1a to 0.5 cm, T1b to 1 cm, T1c to 2 cm), T2 over 2 to 5 cm, T3 over 5 cm, T4 into the chest wall (a), skin (b), both (c) or inflammatory carcinoma (d). Nodes are staged clinically (cN) before any treatment and pathologically (pN) from the sentinel node or clearance: pN1 one to three axillary nodes (pN1mi micrometastases 0.2 to 2 mm), pN2 four to nine, pN3 ten or more or infraclavicular, or axillary plus internal mammary, or supraclavicular nodes. Stage 1A is T1 N0; 1B adds micrometastases; 2A is T0 to T1 N1 or T2 N0; 2B is T2 N1 or T3 N0; 3A is N2 with T0 to T3 or T3 N1; 3B is T4 with N0 to N2; 3C is any N3; stage 4 is any M1. The American Joint Committee on Cancer's 8th edition kept this anatomic stage but added a prognostic stage that folds grade, ER, PR and HER2 status (and, for some hormone receptor-positive tumours, a low Oncotype DX score) into the stage group (Giuliano 2017); in a 3,327-patient MD Anderson cohort the prognostic stage moved 29.5 percent of patients up and 28.1 percent down, and predicted disease-specific survival better than the anatomic stage (C index 0.84 against 0.74), with the same result in 54,727 Californian patients (Weiss 2018). Because grade 3 and receptor negativity count against a tumour, a triple-negative cancer generally carries a higher prognostic than anatomic stage; the UK pathway pages quote the anatomic stage. When chemotherapy is given before surgery, as it is for most stage II and III triple-negative disease, the response at surgery (pathological complete response or residual cancer burden) becomes the stronger prognostic marker (Cortazar 2014; Symmans 2017; the glossary terms).

Screening and prevention. There is no screening test for triple-negative disease as such. The NHS Breast Screening Programme invites everyone registered as female from age 50 (first invitation between 50 and 53) every three years until their 71st birthday, and women 71 or over can ask for screening (NHS). Because triple-negative tumours arrive younger and grow between rounds, a smaller share is screen-detected (Lin 2012; Houssami 2017), which is one reason the family history pathway matters here. NICE CG164 sets the UK rules: GPs refer to a specialist breast or genetics clinic on defined family patterns, and clinicians should seek genetics advice for families containing triple-negative breast cancer under 40, Jewish ancestry, sarcoma under 45 or glioma; genetic testing is offered when the combined BRCA1 and BRCA2 carrier probability is 10 percent or more (calculated with CanRisk, formerly BOADICEA, or the Manchester score); known BRCA1 or BRCA2 carriers are offered annual MRI from 30 to 49 and annual mammography from 40 to 69, TP53 carriers MRI from 20, and MRI is not offered to carriers aged 50 to 69 unless the breasts are dense. In the UK MARIBS study of 649 women at high familial risk, MRI sensitivity was 77 percent against 40 percent for mammography, 92 against 23 percent in BRCA1 carriers (Leach 2005). Risk-reducing surgery: bilateral mastectomy cut breast cancer risk by about 90 percent in BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers in PROSE (1.9 percent against 48.7 percent over a mean 6.4 years; Rebbeck 2004) and pooled relative risk 0.114 in a 15-study meta-analysis, with contralateral mastectomy 0.072 and salpingo-oophorectomy 0.552 for breast cancer overall (Li 2016), though a prospective study of 3,722 carriers found oophorectomy did not lower breast cancer risk in BRCA1 carriers (hazard ratio 0.96) (Kotsopoulos 2017). CG164 restricts risk-reducing mastectomy to a small proportion of women from high-risk families, managed by a multidisciplinary team with genetic counselling, verified family history and reconstruction options discussed. Chemoprevention has a gap that matters for this subtype: NICE offers tamoxifen (premenopausal) or anastrozole (postmenopausal) for five years to women at high risk, and considers them at moderate risk, but tamoxifen had no effect on invasive ER-negative breast cancer in IBIS-I (hazard ratio 1.05 over 16 years; Cuzick 2015) or NSABP P-1 (Fisher 1998), and anastrozole's 49 percent reduction in IBIS-II came from ER-positive disease (54 percent fewer invasive ER-positive cancers, no significant effect on ER-negative cancer; Cuzick 2020); Cancer Research UK says the trial evidence is unclear for women with gene changes. One observational signal runs the other way: tamoxifen after a first breast cancer was associated with a lower contralateral breast cancer risk in BRCA1 (hazard ratio 0.38) and BRCA2 (0.33) carriers regardless of the first tumour's ER status (Phillips 2013). Breastfeeding is the modifiable factor with a specific ER-negative signal (Palmer 2014), and keeping a healthy weight and being physically active are the general measures Cancer Research UK names.

notes: What does triple-negative actually mean? The tested invasive cancer is classified as ER-negative and PR-negative, each below 1 percent nuclear staining, and HER2-negative under the relevant IHC/ISH algorithm. Retain the specimen, score and test-validity information. These test categories do not establish that every receptor molecule is absent or that the cell has no other receptors. ER 1 to 10 percent is ER Low Positive; limited endocrine-benefit evidence and overlap in some cohort features do not make it ER-negative (ASCO/CAP 2020 and 2023).

How common is it? About 10.8 percent of all US breast cancers (SEER 21, 2019 to 2023) and around 15 percent on Cancer Research UK's page; roughly 12 percent in earlier US series (Howlader 2014). It is diagnosed younger: women under 40 have about 1.5 to 2 times the odds of a triple-negative diagnosis (Bauer 2007; Scott 2019).

Why is it more common in Black women? In the United States the rate is 25.7 per 100,000 non-Hispanic Black women against 13.0 for non-Hispanic White women (SEER 21), and in the UK POSH cohort 26.1 percent of Black against 18.6 percent of White young patients had triple-negative tumours (Copson 2014). Reproductive patterns (parity without breastfeeding raises ER-negative risk in African American women, Palmer 2014), ancestry and access all contribute; the causes are not settled (Howard and Olopade 2021).

Should I have a genetic test? NICE says yes for women under 50 with triple-negative disease even without a family history (NG101 1.3.6), and UK mainstream criteria extend testing to all triple-negative disease under 60 (Evans 2024); about 11 percent of unselected triple-negative patients carry a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation and 14.6 percent a mutation in one of 17 genes (Couch 2015). The result changes surgery options, opens olaparib after chemotherapy for high-risk early disease (NICE TA886) and matters for relatives.

Is it more dangerous than other breast cancers? Stage for stage, survival is lower: 78.7 percent five-year relative survival against 95.8 percent for hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative disease in SEER, but 92.8 percent when found while localised. The risk of relapse is concentrated in the first three to five years and is low afterwards (Dent 2007), and a pathological complete response to chemotherapy before surgery carries an excellent outlook (Liedtke 2008; Cortazar 2014).

Why did my treatment start with chemotherapy rather than surgery? For tumours over 2 cm or with node involvement, chemotherapy with pembrolizumab is given first because the response at surgery predicts relapse and directs what follows, and because it raised five-year survival from 81.7 to 86.6 percent in KEYNOTE-522 (Schmid 2024). NICE recommends a platinum, a taxane and an anthracycline in that setting (NG101 1.8, 2025) and pembrolizumab with it (TA851).

Does hormone therapy or tamoxifen have any role? Hormone receptor-negative breast cancer generally does not respond to endocrine treatment. ER Low Positive is a separate positive category with limited benefit data and needs its own clinical interpretation. As prevention, tamoxifen and anastrozole reduced ER-positive but not ER-negative breast cancer in the prevention trials (Cuzick 2015; Fisher 1998; Cuzick 2020), although tamoxifen after a first cancer was associated with fewer contralateral cancers in BRCA carriers (Phillips 2013).

Will screening pick it up? The NHS invites women from 50 to 71 every three years (NHS). Triple-negative cancers are less often screen-detected (29 percent against 48 percent, Lin 2012) because they arise younger and grow between rounds. Known BRCA carriers are offered annual MRI from 30 and mammography from 40 (NICE CG164); anyone with a new breast change should see a GP without waiting for the next screen.

What are the subtypes I might read about? Gene expression divides triple-negative disease into basal-like 1 and 2, mesenchymal and luminal androgen receptor tumours (Lehmann 2016), which respond differently to chemotherapy (pathological complete response 41 percent for basal-like 1, 18 percent for basal-like 2, 29 percent for luminal androgen receptor) but are not used to choose treatment in the NHS. Special histological types such as adenoid cystic and secretory carcinoma are triple-negative but indolent and may need no chemotherapy (Cserni 2021). Each has a page linked from this record.

What is HER2-low and why can it matter within a HER2-negative report? IHC 1+ or IHC 2+/ISH-negative is a HER2-low category used in specified studies and labelling. DESTINY-Breast04 included hormone receptor-negative disease after chemotherapy. The current U.S. T-DXd low-expression breast use requires an advanced-disease setting and specified prior treatment; the separate ultralow use after endocrine therapy requires HR-positive disease. A staining result alone does not establish all the clinical requirements or promise a response.

TNBC is a receptor-test category requiring completed negative ER, PR and HER2 assessments on the relevant invasive tumour. ER and PR below 1% are negative under the standard breast guideline; ER 1% to 10% is ER-low positive. A pending, unknown or uninterpretable result is not negative. HER2 IHC 2+ needs its indicated workup; IHC and ISH measure protein pattern and gene copies respectively. The three completed results are independent observations assembled into a category, not a causal chain or a complete portrait of tumour biology.

NCI describes TNBC as about 15% of breast cancers and more common among younger women, Black women than White women, and people with certain harmful BRCA variants. These are population associations, not proof of origin or an individual forecast. Its tendency toward faster growth or recurrence does not give every tumour the same course. Clinical TNBC is generally an invasive-cancer classification; a description that it is rarely stage 0 does not make an in-situ lesion equivalent to invasive TNBC. Receptor negativity does not mean no treatment targets: some settings use chemotherapy or immunotherapy, and some HER2-low cancers can meet a specified ADC indication.

Keep specimen/block, site and collection date, the individual ER and PR percentages and interpretations, HER2 IHC and any completed ISH result, controls and adequate invasive tumour. Testing consumes sections. An unresolved test needs resolution rather than a negative label. A general RNA classifier cannot replace these clinical assays, and trial-entry thresholds may differ from standard pathology categories. Results from different sites or dates should be compared with that context rather than selecting three negatives from different specimens to invent a single TNBC result.

In a fictional adequately controlled report, ER below 1%, PR below 1% and completed HER2 1+ can be both TNBC and HER2-low. Change only ER to 4% and standard TNBC no longer applies: the result is ER-low positive even if a separate RNA classifier reports basal-like. A basal-marker stain, PAM50 or TNBCtype label does not change those receptor measurements. Neither classification alone supplies stage, grade, immune activity, drug eligibility or an individual treatment-benefit probability.

KEYNOTE-522 studied previously untreated stage II or III TNBC. Pembrolizumab with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab improved overall survival compared with the chemotherapy/placebo regimen in Schmid and colleagues' final report; overall survival was a secondary endpoint. This is evidence for the tested regimen and population. It does not show that every early TNBC has the same benefit or isolate the contribution of each treatment phase.

Frequencies marked cBioPortal were computed from the public API on 24 September 2026 on receptor-defined triple-negative subsets of brca_tcga_pub (123 samples; the same patients read in brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018), brca_metabric (320) and breast_msk_2018 (176), as sample-level counts of non-synonymous mutation, high-level amplification or deep deletion over the subset; they are not the papers' own percentages, which are quoted alongside.

Metastatic samples in breast_msk_2018 (85 of 176) and the 173-gene METABRIC panel make cross-cohort comparison approximate; TMB on the MSK panel is reported as a mutation count, not a per-megabase rate.

Receptor classification, grade and stage describe different features. Triple-negative refers to the ER, PR and HER2 test results; grade describes microscopic features, and stage describes extent together with the factors in the applicable staging system. A grade does not replace receptor testing or establish an individual prognosis. ER 1 to 10 percent is ER Low Positive under ASCO/CAP criteria, with limited endocrine-benefit evidence; it should not be relabelled ER-negative from an average cohort comparison. Trial entry rules require the actual protocol.
records.burden: About 10 to 15 percent of breast cancers: 10.8 percent of all US cases (SEER 21, 2019 to 2023) and around 15 percent on Cancer Research UK's patient page, against 2.43 million breast cancers a year worldwide (GLOBOCAN 2024). Diagnosed younger, about twice as often in Black women (25.7 against 13.0 per 100,000 in the United States) and in most breast cancers arising in BRCA1 carriers.
